The anterior opening border is limited by ligaments and joint anatomy, not by the teeth.

pb-div2: Distal molars on both sides make it Class II; a square arch, retroclined centrals, flared laterals and a deep overlap make it division 2.

The findings center on posterior teeth hitting first in CR, not on the steepness of canine guidance.
an-ginglymus: Ginglymus is a synovial joint with uniaxial hinge movement in one plane: elbow, knee and finger joints.
Free gliding between flat surfaces (wrist, ankle, spine) describes an arthrodial joint.
Rotation around a single pivot describes a pivot (trochoid) joint like the atlantoaxial, not a ginglymus.
An immovable fibrous joint like a suture is a synarthrosis, not a ginglymus, which is a movable hinge.
an-arthrodial: Sliding of the condyle and disc down the eminence (translation) is the arthrodial, gliding part.
Rotation about the hinge axis is the ginglymus (hinge) part of the joint.
Elevation by the masseter is a muscle action, not one of the joint's two movement types.
Opening by the digastric is a muscle action; the gliding component is translation in the upper compartment.
an-one-bone: The mandible articulates at both TMJs, so nothing the left side does is free of the right side, and vice versa.
The two compartments split rotation and translation, but the phrase refers to one mandible joining two joints.
The disc functions as a third bone, which makes the TMJ compound; that is a different idea from one bone, two joints.
Each side is one joint, divided by the disc into compartments; the two joints are the left and right TMJs.
an-iz: The condyle normally sits in the thin, avascular, aneural intermediate zone.
The posterior border is the thickest part of the disc; the condyle sits in front of it.
The anterior border is thick and lies ahead of the condyle in the closed position.
The retrodiscal tissues are vascular and innervated; loading them is painful, not normal.
an-disc-borders: Sagittally the posterior border is the thickest, even thicker than the anterior border.
The anterior border is considerably thicker than the intermediate zone, but thinner than the posterior border.
The intermediate zone is the thinnest part, where the condyle sits.
The disc is biconcave, with thin and thick parts, not uniform.
an-disc-medial: The disc is slightly thicker medially, so a displaced disc tends to slip forward or medially.
The disc is thicker medially, not laterally, and displaced discs go forward or medially.
The thicker medial side is right, but displacement goes forward or medially, not laterally.
The disc is thicker medially, and displacement is forward or medial, not posterior.
an-meniscus: A meniscus is crescent-shaped with a convex and a concave side, as in the knee; the TMJ disc is biconcave.
A meniscus is fibrocartilage, not bone; the difference is its crescent shape.
The TMJ disc's intermediate zone is avascular, so it isn't fully vascular; the difference is shape.
Menisci occur in the knee, not only in hinge joints; the issue is shape, not joint type.
an-compound: A compound joint needs at least three bones; the TMJ has two, but the disc functions as the third.
Hinge plus glide is true of the TMJ but explains ginglymoarthrodial, not compound.
One bone forming two joints makes the TMJs bilateral, not compound.
All synovial joints have bone covered by articular tissue; that doesn't define a compound joint.
an-compartments: Hinge rotation is between condyle and disc (lower compartment); sliding is between disc and temporal bone (upper).
This is reversed: rotation is in the lower (disc-to-condyle) compartment, translation in the upper.
Only translation occurs in the upper compartment; rotation happens below the disc.
Only rotation occurs in the lower compartment; translation happens above the disc.
an-retrodiscal: Retrodiscal tissues are loaded with blood vessels and nerves, so functioning on them causes substantial pain.
The avascular, aneural part is the intermediate zone; the retrodiscal tissues are the opposite.
The superior lateral pterygoid attaches to the disc anteriorly, not behind it.
Rotation in the lower compartment is between condyle and disc, not in the retrodiscal tissues.
an-lamina: The superior retrodiscal lamina is elastic and helps pull the disc back.
The inferior retrodiscal lamina is collagenous, not elastic.
Only the inferior lamina is purely collagenous; the superior one is elastic.
The superior retrodiscal lamina provides the elastic pull; the capsular ligament isn't the source.
an-surfaces: The surfaces are lined with a resilient, collagenous, fluid-filled articular covering that can swell and shrink.
Hydroxyapatite is the mineral of enamel and bone; joint surfaces are lined with soft collagenous tissue.
Retrodiscal tissues lie behind the disc and don't cover the articulating surfaces.
Synovial membrane lines the joint spaces, but the articulating surfaces have their own collagenous covering.
an-load: Biting needs something to pivot against: the seated joint. So the joint seats and is loaded whenever the elevators contract.
The old belief that the joint carries little force is outdated; the disc doesn't prevent loading the condyle.
The joint is loaded in everyone who bites and chews, not only in patients missing posterior teeth.
Every crushing bite loads the joint, not just night clenching.
an-capsular: The capsular ligament wraps the whole joint like a wall and keeps the condyle from dropping far out of the fossa.
The sphenomandibular ligament runs from the sphenoid spine to the lingula and limits opening and forward motion.
The lateral discal ligament ties the disc to the lateral pole of the condyle; it doesn't encase the joint.
The stylomandibular ligament runs from the styloid to the ramus and limits forward motion; it doesn't encase the joint.
an-discal: The discal ligaments tie the disc to the condyle's medial and lateral poles, keeping it on the condyle while allowing rotation.
Limiting opening and forward motion is the job of the stylomandibular and sphenomandibular ligaments.
Limiting posterior movement is the job of the TM ligament's inner horizontal portion.
The discal ligaments attach the disc to the condyle, not to the eminence.
an-stylo: The stylomandibular and sphenomandibular ligaments limit opening and forward motion of the mandible.
The TM ligament limits rotational opening (outer oblique) and posterior movement (inner horizontal), not protrusion.
The discal ligaments keep the disc on the condyle; they don't limit protrusion.
The capsular ligament encases the joint, and the collateral (discal) ligaments hold the disc; neither is the protrusion limiter.
an-tml-outer: The outer oblique portion limits rotational opening, which is why pure rotation stops at about 20-25 mm.
Limiting posterior movement of the condyle and disc is the inner horizontal portion's job.
Lateral disc displacement is resisted by the discal (collateral) ligaments.
Forward movement is limited by the stylomandibular and sphenomandibular ligaments.
an-tml-inner: A blow to the chin drives the mandible back; the inner horizontal TM ligament limits that and protects the retrodiscal tissues.
The stylomandibular ligament limits forward movement, not backward displacement.
The outer oblique portion limits rotational opening, not posterior displacement.
The sphenomandibular ligament limits opening and forward motion, not posterior displacement.
an-openlock: Gentle downward pressure on the buccal shelf distracts the condyle so it can pop back behind the eminence.
Pushing posteriorly drives the condyle against the eminence; Dr. Givan says not to push it back.
The patient can't close, and clenching won't bring the condyle down past the eminence.
Dr. Givan's fix is distracting the condyle via the buccal shelf, not injecting a muscle.
an-pull: Muscles can only contract, so movement needs agonist and antagonist pairs working together; the opposing muscle never fully turns off.
Opening is active, driven by the inferior lateral pterygoid and the suprahyoids, not gravity alone.
The masseter closes; it can't push the jaw open, which is why openers are needed.
Ligaments limit movement; they don't act as springs pushing the mandible back.
an-design: Innervation is not a factor in muscle design on the handout, and Dr. Givan said he won't test innervation.
Surface available for attachment is one of the handout's four design factors.
Speed of contraction is one of the handout's four design factors.
Range and force of contraction are two of the handout's four design factors.
an-masseter-oi: The masseter runs from the zygomatic arch and malar process to the angle of the ramus.
Temporal fossa and fascia to the coronoid process is the temporalis.
Lateral pterygoid plate to the medial ramus is the medial pterygoid.
The greater wing of the sphenoid to the condylar region is the lateral pterygoid, not the masseter.
an-masseter-bellies: The superficial (power) belly elevates with some protrusion; the deep belly elevates with retrusion.
Both bellies elevate; the superficial adds protrusion and the deep adds retrusion, not the reverse.
Both elevate, but they also differ: superficial adds protrusion, deep adds retrusion.
Neither belly depresses the mandible; the masseter is a closing muscle.
an-masseter-seat: The masseter's fibers run up and forward, the same direction as CR, so contracting it seats the condyles against the eminence.
Seating is anterior-superior against the eminence; pulling the condyle back into the retrodiscal tissues is the opposite.
The masseter doesn't act on the disc; it lifts the mandible up and forward.
The masseter seats the joints whenever it contracts, whether or not the teeth are in MIP.
an-temporalis: The fan-shaped temporalis inserts on the small coronoid, not a power position: it is the jaw's fast positioner, elevating and retracting.
The power closers are the masseter and medial pterygoid; the temporalis is mainly a positioner.
The temporalis elevates; depression is done by the inferior lateral pterygoid and the suprahyoids.
Stabilizing the disc during closure is the superior lateral pterygoid's job.
an-temporalis-parts: The posterior, more horizontal fibers retrude the mandible, with some elevation.
The anterior fibers mainly elevate the mandible.
The middle fibers elevate with only some retrusion; the posterior fibers are the main retruders.
The temporalis does retrude, through its posterior fibers; it is on the exam slide for retrusion.
an-zygoma: Dr. Givan says the temporalis is so important that we build a tunnel around it: the arch lets the coronoid move as it contracts.
The parotid duct runs over the masseter, not through the arch; the arch tunnels the temporalis.
The disc sits inside the joint capsule; the zygomatic arch tunnels the temporalis insertion.
The masseteric nerve isn't what the arch is said to protect; it tunnels the temporalis and coronoid.
an-lp-sup: The superior head inserts on the capsule and disc and works during closure, stabilizing the disc against the retrodiscal lamina's elastic pull.
The pterygoid fovea, active in opening and protrusion, describes the inferior head.
The coronoid process is the temporalis insertion, and retrusion is posterior temporalis and deep masseter.
The medial ramus is the medial pterygoid's insertion; the superior lateral pterygoid goes to the disc.
an-lp-inf: The inferior head pulls the condyle forward, down and medially: both sides together give opening and protrusion.
The superior head is inactive while opening; it works during closure.
The medial pterygoid elevates the mandible; it doesn't open it.
The posterior temporalis retrudes the mandible, the opposite of protrusion.
an-lp-unilateral: One inferior lateral pterygoid pulls its condyle forward and medially, swinging the chin to the opposite side: right contracts, jaw goes left.
Contracting the right one moves the jaw to the left, not the right.
Straight forward needs both inferior lateral pterygoids contracting together.
The lateral pterygoid pulls forward; retrusion comes from the posterior temporalis and deep masseter.
an-mp: The medial pterygoid arises from the medial surface of the lateral pterygoid plate, inserts on the medial ramus and elevates.
The lateral surface of the lateral pterygoid plate is the origin of the inferior lateral pterygoid, which protrudes.
Inserting on the disc and stabilizing it in closure describes the superior lateral pterygoid.
The coronoid insertion and retrusion describe the temporalis.
an-sling: The masseter outside and the medial pterygoid inside the ramus grab the mandible together: the pterygomasseteric sling.
The temporalis inserts on the coronoid; the sling pairs the masseter with the medial pterygoid.
The two lateral pterygoid heads go to the disc and condyle, not around the ramus.
The digastric and mylohyoid are suprahyoid openers, not part of the sling.
an-ex-elev: Exam slide, elevation: temporalis, medial pterygoid and masseter.
The inferior lateral pterygoid and suprahyoids open (depress) the mandible.
Superficial masseter plus inferior lateral pterygoid is the protrusion pair on the slide.
Posterior temporalis plus deep masseter is the retrusion pair on the slide.
an-ex-dep: Exam slide, depression: the lateral pterygoid (inferior belly) with the suprahyoid and infrahyoid groups.
The temporalis and masseter are elevators that close the jaw.
The superficial masseter and medial pterygoid are elevators, not openers.
The superior lateral pterygoid is inactive during opening; it works in closure.
an-ex-pro: Exam slide, protrusion: the inferior lateral pterygoid and the superficial masseter.
Posterior temporalis plus deep masseter retrude the mandible.
The medial pterygoid and temporalis are on the slide as elevators, not protruders.
The digastric and mylohyoid are suprahyoids that help open the jaw.
an-ex-retr: Exam slide, retrusion: the temporalis (posterior, horizontal fibers) and the deep masseter.
The inferior lateral pterygoid and superficial masseter protrude, the opposite movement.
The medial pterygoid elevates, and the superior lateral pterygoid stabilizes the disc in closure.
The supra- and infrahyoids open the jaw; they are not on the slide for retrusion.
an-ex-right: To the right: right temporalis and right masseter on the working side, with the LEFT lateral and LEFT medial pterygoids pulling from the opposite side.
This set moves the mandible to the LEFT, the mirror image.
Both lateral pterygoids contracting equally give straight protrusion, not a move to one side.
The right pterygoids would swing the chin to the left; the left ones pull it right.
ex-left: The left lateral pterygoid pulls the left condyle forward and medially, swinging the chin to the RIGHT, so it doesn't help move left.
The right lateral pterygoid swings the chin to the left, so it is on the slide for a left movement.
The left temporalis works on the left (working) side in a left movement.
The right medial pterygoid pulls from the opposite side to swing the chin left.
an-suprahyoid: Digastric, geniohyoid, mylohyoid and stylohyoid form the suprahyoid (inframandibular) group that helps open the jaw.
Sternohyoid, omohyoid, sternothyroid and thyrohyoid are the infrahyoids, which stabilize the hyoid.
These four are the muscles of mastication (supramandibular group).
The sternocleidomastoid and trapezius are neck muscles that maintain head position.
an-infrahyoid: The hyoid floats, so the infrahyoids contract rigidly below it to make it a fixed base the suprahyoids can pull against.
The infrahyoids don't attach to the mandible; the suprahyoids pull it down once the hyoid is fixed.
The elevators bring the teeth into MIP; in swallowing the infrahyoids relax so the hyoid can move forward.
Protruding the tongue isn't their job; they stabilize the hyoid.
an-digastric: With the hyoid fixed, the anterior belly starts opening and the posterior belly continues it: a key opening muscle.
The digastric is an opener; elevation is done by the masseter, temporalis and medial pterygoid.
Retrusion is done by the posterior temporalis and deep masseter.
Disc stabilization is the superior lateral pterygoid's job.
an-mylohyoid: The mylohyoid forms the muscular floor of the mouth and, by shortening, helps depress the mandible.

cc-cingulum: The tongue thrust pushes on the extra cingulum bulk from behind, so the tooth itself is pushed labially.
The added bulk is on the maxillary tooth and the thrust pushes it outward; lingual tipping of the lower incisors isn't the risk.
The incisal edge position on "f" isn't changed by cingulum bulk.
The curve of Spee is a posterior curve and isn't affected by cingulum contour.
cc-lip-bulge: A gingival bulge usually means the lab had no room because the tooth was under-prepared.
The bulge creates excess lip support; it isn't compensating for too much.
Incisal edge length has nothing to do with a bulge near the gingiva.
Vertical overlap concerns the incisal third, not a cervical bulge.
cc-pb-sda: With no posterior support the anteriors are being destroyed, so support comes first; to the second premolars may be enough on a limited budget.
Veneers without posterior support would fail like the original teeth are failing; support first, disclusion second.
Adjusting anterior guidance can't help while the anteriors carry all the load without back teeth.
Instrument choice doesn't address the real problem, the lack of posterior support.
ap-schemes: The three accepted schemes are balanced occlusion (dentures), mutually protected occlusion and group function.
These mix one scheme (canine guidance) with contact types (cusp-fossa, cusp-marginal ridge, tripodization).
Conformative and reorganized are restorative approaches, and neuromuscular is a philosophy, not an occlusal scheme.
These are contact concepts and a CR-to-MICP slide, not occlusal schemes.
ap-copy: With no signs or symptoms, copy the existing guidance (group function) when restoring.
Canine guidance isn't automatically better; converting a healthy occlusion is not conformative dentistry.
Balanced occlusion is for dentures, not natural teeth.
Removing #6's lateral contact changes a healthy, functioning group function scheme.
ap-mip: MIP is the end of the chewing cycle, where force peaks and the mandible is stabilized to swallow; it changes as the occlusion changes.
MIP is not stable long term; it changes whenever the occlusion changes, so it is not unquestionable.
MIP is a tooth-determined position; CR is a joint-determined position, and the two often differ.
MIP is used every day in natural dentitions, not just for dentures.
ap-contacts-day: 17.5 minutes of daily MIP contact is about 1,800 chewing strokes plus 500 swallowing contacts.
Reversed: 1,800 are the chewing strokes and 500 the swallowing contacts.
590 is the total swallows per day and 146 the swallows at meals, not tooth contacts in MIP.
These numbers are about ten times too high for one day.
ap-working-check: On the working side, check the guiding teeth's mobility (do they need splinting?) and whether the glide is smooth or restricted.
Shade has nothing to do with whether working-side contacts are healthy.
VDR and freeway space are measured at rest, not in a guiding excursion.
The curve of Wilson isn't what you check for working-side guidance.
ap-nw: Non-working side contacts tend to guide the mandible during lateral excursion.
A non-working contact doesn't protect the canine; it takes over guidance on the wrong side.
Non-working contacts are interferences and don't improve chewing.
Non-working contacts are not described as stabilizing the disc.
ap-pdl: The PDL's sensory elements can detect about 20 µm between the teeth.
200 µm is ten times thicker than the PDL threshold.
2 mm is a hundred times larger than what the PDL can detect.
0.2 µm is far below the roughly 20 µm threshold.
ap-protrusive: Posterior protrusive interferences must be eliminated before the anterior teeth are restored.
Posterior protrusive interferences don't protect the crowns; they take over guidance and must go first.
Adding posterior protrusive contacts creates more interferences.
Copying an interference into new restorations keeps the problem.
ap-conform: Not a localized adjustment: moving the whole occlusion to CR is the reorganized approach.
Shortening an opposing cusp is one of the localized conformative adjustments.
Eliminating non-working interferences is one of the localized conformative adjustments.
Removing a deflective contact on the tooth to be restored is one of the localized conformative adjustments.
ap-reorg: Reorganized goals: a reproducible starting point (joints seated in CR), an even stable occlusion, no iatrogenic deflective contacts.
Copying MIP with local adjustments is the conformative approach.
Reorganizing doesn't require raising the vertical in every case.
Bilateral balance is for dentures, not a goal for natural teeth.
ap-cr-when: Use a CR record when reorganizing and when mounting diagnostic casts for treatment planning.
A conformative single crown uses an MIP record or hand articulation.
Working casts for a healthy occlusion are mounted in MIP, used as minimally as needed.
Canine guidance has nothing to do with choosing a CR record.
ap-bimanual: Bimanual manipulation seats the condyles with an upward, anterior force while the teeth are held apart, then the record is taken.
Forcing the jaw back as far as it goes recreates the old RUM position, not today's anterior-superior CR.
The TENS myocentric point is neuromuscular and is not CR.
A full-arch bite in MIP records the tooth position, not CR, and full-arch records add mounting errors.
ap-materials: Not a bite registration material: alginate (irreversible hydrocolloid) is an impression material.
PVS (Regisil) is one of the listed registration materials.
Aluwax is one of the listed registration materials.
ZOE plaster is one of the listed registration materials.
ap-wax: Wax chilled with the syringe hardens in 1-2 seconds; PVS takes 20-30 seconds, and patients move during that time.
PVS is an excellent impression material; the advantage is wax's fast set, not superior accuracy.
Wax records still need trimming like any other record.
A material can't find CR by itself; CR comes from how you guide the jaw.
ap-errors: The two errors: a full-arch registration (material where teeth should touch) and untrimmed excess (the record rocks and can't be verified).
Wax is one of Dr. Givan's preferred materials, and a semi-adjustable articulator isn't an error.
Patient posture is not one of the two errors named.
Trimming to the cusp tips is the right way to trim; it isn't an error.
ap-mip-record: A correct MIP record sits only where teeth don't touch, trimmed to the cusp tips and kept off soft tissue.
Full-arch coverage is a named error: it puts material between teeth that should touch.
MIP means teeth in contact, so a record that separates them is no longer MIP.
Soft tissue and palate coverage make the record rock and add error.
ap-elastomer: This is the wrong step: keep a constant occlusal pressure while the material sets; releasing it early ruins the record.
Constant occlusal pressure during setting is correct technique.
Trimming excess with a scalpel before mounting is correct technique.
Holding pressure on the casts while mounting prevents rebound and is correct technique.
ap-intra: The restoration should contact at the same time as the other teeth in MIP.
Infraocclusion lets teeth supererupt into poor contacts; it is not protective.
Non-working contacts on a restoration are interferences to avoid.
A restoration hitting first is a high spot or deflective contact.
ap-infra: Out of occlusion, the tooth or its opponent supererupts and never erupts into a good contact, so interferences develop.
Infraocclusion removes contact from the restoration; it doesn't increase bite force on it.
Leaving a tooth out of occlusion does not cause immediate pulpal pain.
Infraocclusion doesn't move the condyle; the problem is drifting and supereruption.
ap-large: Before a large restoration, look before you cut: check for an over-erupted opposing cusp, plane violations and NW contacts, and adjust first.
One large restoration calls for localized adjustment, not reorganizing the quadrant.
Raising the vertical isn't called for to place one restoration.
A fully adjustable articulator isn't needed for a single intracoronal restoration.
ap-plunger: A plunger cusp is an over-erupted cusp that breaks the plane of occlusion and plunges into the opposing tooth or embrasure.
A ground-flat non-centric cusp is not a plunger cusp.
That describes a normal Class I centric holding cusp, not a plunger.
Swallowing contacts are not what defines a plunger cusp.
ap-multi: Multiple large posterior restorations in quadrants call for the reorganized approach with high-strength materials.
Conformative suits multiple small restorations, not many large ones.
Infraocclusion is never the goal; it leads to supereruption.
ap-single: A single bounded crown is conformative: hand articulation (or PVS/Aluwax), no face-bow, a hinge articulator.
Reorganizing with CR and a face-bow is far more than a single bounded crown needs.
A fully adjustable articulator with a pantograph is not needed for one bounded crown.
Full-arch records are a named error, and a semi-adjustable is only rarely used here.
ap-tryin: Seat the crown fully first: check proximal contacts and complete seating, since tight contacts keep it from seating.
Shade is not what must be verified before occlusion; seating comes first.
VDR is a rest measurement, not part of crown try-in.
The patient's chewing side doesn't need to be checked before occlusion; seating does.
ap-end: At the end of the arch, adjust any retruded deflective contact first and mount with a registration, since hand-articulated casts drop back.
An end-of-arch crown does need a registration because the cast drops posteriorly without one.
A single end-of-arch crown is usually still conformative, not reorganized.
Infraocclusion lets teeth supererupt; the last tooth needs proper contact too.
ap-3unit: A three-unit bounded bridge: conformative, a good opposing plane, and a semi-adjustable (arcon) articulator.
Reorganizing with a fully adjustable articulator is not needed for a three-unit bridge in every case.
A hinge articulator is only sometimes acceptable here; semi-adjustable is recommended.
A registration (PVS or Aluwax) is used to mount a three-unit bridge.
ap-hinge: Dr. Givan says the hinge articulator's advantage is entirely to the laboratory.
The dentist actually makes more adjustments, because a small hinge moves on arcs unlike the patient's.
Crowns from a small hinge fit the patient's movement worse, so the patient gains nothing.
The benefit isn't shared; it goes only to the lab.
ap-quad: Not needed: bilateral balanced contacts are a denture scheme, not a step to fix the opposing plane.
Crown lengthening may be needed to give the opposing arch a good occlusal plane.
Crowns on opposing teeth may be needed to correct the opposing plane.
Root canal therapy is on the lecture's list with crown lengthening and opposing crowns, so it may be needed first.
ap-4unit: A four-unit posterior bridge replaces about half the occlusion, so what goes back must be decided, not just copied from MIP.
That's exactly his warning: it is not like a single bounded crown, since half the MIP is gone.
Bilateral balance is for dentures, not fixed bridges.
A bridge this size definitely needs an occlusal record.
ap-c3: For a Class III, copy the existing contacts and keep centric and protrusive contact off the composite where possible.
Putting all centric contact on the composite is the opposite of the goal; composite won't last like tooth.
Guidance on a Class III composite would load the weaker material.
Leaving the tooth out of occlusion lets it drift or supererupt.
ap-c4: Share centric and protrusive contact between tooth and composite to reduce fracture and differential wear.
All contact on the composite is "a recipe for disaster."
Taking contact off the natural tooth puts it all on the composite.
Canine guidance belongs on canines, not on a restored incisor.
ap-single-ant: Fix posterior deflective contacts that slide the mandible forward into the incisors, especially after a previous fracture.
A shortened dental arch is an acceptable endpoint, not a problem to fix before an anterior crown.
Healthy group function should be copied, not converted to canine guidance.
A 3 mm vertical overlap is not a posterior problem that must be corrected.
ap-agt: A custom anterior guide table is needed when restoring both maxillary centrals or one or both canines.
A single lateral or a premolar crown doesn't need one; laterals do little of the guiding.
Posterior crowns don't set the anterior guidance.
A Class III composite doesn't change the guidance pathways.
ap-agt-time: To copy the guidance unchanged, make the custom guide impression before the anterior teeth are prepared.
After preparation the original guiding surfaces are gone.
After the finals are seated it is too late; the table guides how they are built.
Copying still needs the table; it is how the existing guidance is carried into the new crowns.
ap-weeks: At least about three weeks for a mild, asymptomatic patient, and months for a bruxer.
One day is too short to test new guidance.
A year is far longer than needed for a mild case.
Same-day finals skip the test period that proves the provisionals work.
ap-css: Closest speaking space is 1-2 mm between the incisal edges while the patient says "s" (counting 60-70).
2-6 mm is the freeway space at rest, not the closest speaking space on "s."
"Ah" opens the mouth wide; closest speaking space is measured on "s."
Teeth don't touch on "s"; there should be about 1-2 mm of space.
ap-mobility: A natural tooth moves about 28 µm apically into its PDL; an implant moves only 2-3 µm through bone microstrain.
Reversed: the tooth moves 28 µm, the implant only 2-3 µm.
Both values are too high for apical movement under about 10 lb.
An implant has no PDL, so it moves far less than a natural tooth.
ap-imp-mip: Very light on casual closure and equal on a firm clench, because the teeth sink into their PDL and the implant doesn't.
Heavier implant contact overloads the implant, which has no PDL cushion.
Leaving it with no contact lets the opposing tooth supererupt.
Posterior implants should avoid excursive contact, not have it only in excursions.
ap-shim: Light closure: shimstock holds on #12 and #14 and drags on #13; on a clench all three hold.
On a clench the teeth sink into their PDL, so all three should hold; #12 and #14 shouldn't pull through.
On a firm clench the teeth should hold shimstock, not let it pull through.
On light closure the implant should be slightly lighter, dragging rather than holding firmly.
ap-imp-ant: Skip immediate canine disclusion on an implant (no PDL proprioception); share the load with natural teeth.
An implant lacks a PDL, so it shouldn't carry full canine guidance alone.
Removing all anterior contact would lose the anterior guidance entirely.
ap-imp-post-ex: Posterior implants should avoid excursive contact if possible, in a mutually protected occlusion.
Working contacts on a posterior implant are avoided.
Non-working contacts are interferences, and especially unwanted on implants.
An implant contacting first overloads it; it can't sense or cushion force.
ap-diag: Compare the CO and MIP contacts and look for wear, fracture and mobility; a big discrepancy with damage says conformative isn't safe.
Group function is a perfectly healthy scheme; canine guidance isn't the test for conformative safety.
Freeway space doesn't tell you whether copying MIP is safe.
Having all teeth doesn't rule out wear, fracture or mobility.
ap-pb-crown: Asymptomatic with healthy canine guidance: stay conformative, but first fix #30's over-erupted (plunger) cusp, then use an MIP record.
A healthy, asymptomatic patient needs no full-mouth reorganization.
Infraocclusion would let teeth supererupt, and #30 has already over-erupted.
Canine guidance already protects the posteriors; adding working contacts on #3 makes an interference.
ap-pb-agt: Restoring both centrals and both canines needs a custom guide, and copying requires capturing it before #6-11 are cut.
After preparation, the guidance she likes is gone.
After cementation is too late; the table guides how the crowns are built.
Copying still needs a custom anterior guide table, because both centrals and canines are being restored.
ap-pb-c4: Edge to edge with a history of fracture: share centric and protrusive contacts between composite and natural tooth.
All protrusive contact on the composite is "a recipe for disaster," especially with prior fractures.
Leaving #8 out of contact lets it drift or supererupt and shifts load elsewhere.
All the anterior guidance on #8 would overload the restoration.
pb-upright: Contacts set with the chair reclined can shift anteriorly once he sits up; upright posture changes the path of closure.
A direct composite has no MIP record or lab step, so a record taken in CR can't be the cause.
A thin composite would chip or fracture; flexing doesn't make one tooth hit first.
A 2-6 mm freeway space is normal rest posture, not a high contact.
cs-upright: Adjust where the problem shows: upright, the posture he eats in, until shimstock holds on #18 and #20 again.
A high restoration is a deflective contact; it doesn't wear in, and the PDL senses about 20 µm.
Checking reclined again repeats the original error: the contacts only looked even lying back.
The fix belongs on the new restoration, not on the healthy opposing tooth.
cs-reorg: A big deviating slide, wear, fractures and posterior crowns in several quadrants call for reorganizing from seated joints with a CR record.
Conformative copying of MIP is for healthy, asymptomatic occlusions; his is unstable.
A full-arch registration is a classic record error: material between teeth that should touch.
An MIP record would copy the unstable position the reorganized approach is meant to replace.
cs-fricative: On "f" the incisal edge should lightly touch the wet-dry line; pressing into the lip means the crowns are too long.
Too short shows as being unable to make the "f" sound, not as the lip feeling pushed out.
The closest speaking space is checked with "s", not "f".
The edges should only lightly touch the lower lip; pressing into it is the sign of crowns that are too long.
cs-trauma: Fremitus and mobility with healthy probing point to force from the slide into the incisors; correct that deflective contact first.
Splinting supports the teeth but leaves the force that keeps breaking #8 in place.
Probing depths are 1-3 mm with no bleeding: this isn't periodontal disease, so surgery treats the wrong problem.
A bulkier crown still takes the same force from the slide and will fracture again.
cs-nw: In a left excursion the right side is non-working; a newly added non-working contact on #3 must be removed while keeping its MIP contacts.
Group function is a working-side scheme; in a left excursion #3 is on the non-working side.
Patients can adapt to old non-working contacts, but not to one introduced in an afternoon; the new mobility is the warning.
The blue MIP contacts aren't the problem, and a full-arch registration is a record error, not a fix.
cs-pro: Posterior protrusive interferences must be eliminated before restoring the anterior teeth.
Steeper guidance can't clear a badly tipped molar, and veneers asked to do it will fail.
Balanced occlusion is for dentures; in natural teeth, molar contacts in protrusion are interferences.
Splinting treats mobility, not the interference itself.
cs-implant: An implant has no PDL, so it should be light on casual closure, equal on a clench, and out of excursions.
Shimstock holding on the implant at light closure means the crown is too heavy, not that it's right.
No contact at all lets the opposing tooth supererupt; the goal is light, not none.
Posterior implants should avoid contact in excursions; the excursive mark has to go.
cs-implant6: An anterior implant shares working contacts with the natural teeth (group function) instead of guiding alone.
Steep canine guidance would put all the excursive force on the one tooth with no ligament or proprioception.
Keeping out of every excursion is the rule for posterior implants, not anterior ones.
Anterior implants get a very light centric contact on casual closure; a heavy one is backwards.
cs-worn: Inadequate anterior guidance is rebuilt by testing: wax-up at a tentative VDO, provisionals worn for months, then a guide table from them.
A guide table from the worn teeth copies the guidance he has already lost.
Delivering finals in one visit skips the test drive the provisionals provide.
The 2-6 mm freeway space is normal rest posture, not a target to open the VDO by.
cs-record: A full-arch, untrimmed record holds the casts apart; a small record over the prep, trimmed to cusp tips, keeps teeth that touch in contact.
Slow setting isn't the problem, and a full-arch record of any material repeats the same error.
The crown fits the mounted casts, so the error came in with the record, not the lab.
Clenching harder doesn't fix material sitting between teeth that should touch.
cs-group6: #6 has lost much of its periodontal support, so group function shares the working load with #7 and #5.
Copying the existing guidance applies only without signs or symptoms; #6 has deep pockets, mobility and pain.
Balanced occlusion is for dentures; left molar contacts in a right excursion are non-working interferences.
Letting the molars guide puts the excursive force on the teeth least suited to it.
dn-goal: A denture floats on the tissues, so its occlusion exists to keep it in the mouth while the patient functions.
A complete denture has no abutment teeth; directing forces axially is a dentate goal.
Anterior guidance is avoided in dentures: protruding on the front teeth tips the denture out.
MIP is a neuromuscular position learned from the natural teeth; it is gone with them.
dn-balance: Balance is the opposite of tipping: contacts on both sides at once keep the one-piece denture seated.
Balance is about where the contacts are, not how much force each molar takes.
Matching guidance angles isn't the meaning; balance is contact on both sides to stop tipping.
Tooth heights are esthetic choices; balance means resisting tipping.
dn-hist-role: Early dentures were carved mostly for esthetics; occlusion played practically no role.
Hinges only let the jaws open and close; balance came with Bonwill and Gysi much later.
Canine guidance is a 20th-century idea for natural teeth, not early dentures.
Springs held the upper and lower pieces apart and in place; there was no occlusion to balance.
dn-bonwill: Bonwill set teeth so they stayed touching, the first real denture occlusion: the father of articulation.
Vulcanite, a sulfur-cured rubber base, wasn't Bonwill's contribution.
dn-gysi: Gysi perfected balanced occlusion; his Trubyte teeth are still sold.
Hanau, an engineer, coined the resilient-like effect and simplified building balance.
Fauchard, the father of dentistry, made sprung dentures with no occlusion.
dn-temperament: The temperamental theory matched teeth to personality, and molds are still called soft or bold.
Geometric form matches tooth shape to the face: square, tapering, ovoid.
Berry's ratio sizes the central incisor from the bizygomatic width.
Hanau's quint is the five determinants of balanced occlusion.
dn-implant-why: Edentulism drove implants: keeping dentures in, especially the lower one.
Single-tooth implants came later; they weren't what drove the development.
Orthodontic anchorage wasn't the driver; edentulous patients who couldn't eat were.
dn-one-tooth: Each denture is one piece, so its teeth never work independently.
Denture teeth have various cusp forms; the phrase is about the denture moving as one unit.
Contacts are spread over the posterior teeth, not carried by the first molars.
Dentures contact at many points; the phrase means each denture acts as a single unit.
dn-proprio: The teeth and periodontal tissues gave proprioception; without them patients only vaguely sense position.
CR is still there and fairly easy to find: the muscles seat the joints.
The joints and their discs are unchanged by tooth loss.
The brainstem's pattern generator still runs chewing; the feedback from the teeth is what's missing.
dn-hold: Muscle control is likely the most important factor; some patients keep even poor dentures in.
Suction helps, but it depends on fit and is lost with the first hot sip.
Adhesion and cohesion help but depend on the saliva and aren't strong enough during function.
The seal helps retention of a heat-processed denture; it isn't the main factor.
dn-fit: All of them require good fit: misfit and short borders let air in and break the seal.
Cusp angle shapes the occlusion, not the seal under the base.
Condylar guidance is an articulator setting; it doesn't create suction.
Anterior overlap is esthetic and occlusal; it doesn't affect suction.
dn-border: The peripheral border is the flange's extent, at the moving and non-moving tissue boundary.
The posterior palatal seal is at the back of the maxillary denture, not the flange's limit.
The denture base is the whole plastic part fitting the tissues.
The buccal shelf is a mandibular support area.
dn-pps: Heat-processed resin shrinks; the seal presses into compressible tissue at the back to keep the fit.
It sits at the back of the palate, nowhere near the anterior teeth.
Support comes from the palate itself; the seal is about keeping the fit despite shrinkage.
The seal is at the soft palate, not a tongue barrier.
dn-articulator: The resilient-like effect: the tissue sinks under each contact, so the denture moves and misleads you.
Opening isn't the problem; the moving denture is.
Paper marks denture teeth; the marks are just unreliable because the denture tips.
CR is fairly easy to find in denture patients.
dn-resorb-maxpost: Maxillary posterior bone resorbs upward and toward the midline.
Downward is the mandible; the maxilla goes up and in.
The maxilla resorbs inward, not outward.
Downward and forward is the mandibular anterior.
dn-resorb-mand: The mandible resorbs down and out, so at tooth level it ends up larger.
Upward and inward describes the maxilla, which gets smaller.
Width changes too: down and out makes the mandible larger.
The mandibular anterior goes down and forward, so it isn't narrower in front.
dn-crossbite: Teeth go near the ridge, so a crossbite is often needed, and it's fine.
Cantilevering teeth off the ridge adds leverage and tipping.
Moving the teeth inside the ridge just to avoid a crossbite isn't the rule; they follow the ridge.
Taller cusps add lateral force, the opposite of what a resorbed patient needs.
dn-tongue: The tongue hypertrophies into the space where the teeth were, mostly troubling the lower denture.
It grows, not shrinks, after tooth loss.
It fills the space and presses on the denture; it doesn't retract.
It isn't losing tone; its size is the problem.
dn-recent: Plenty of bone can leave too little interarch space for the base and teeth.
Firm ridges with plenty of bone help; space is the problem.
The tongue grows over time; that isn't why recent extractions are hard.
CR can be recorded; the space for the denture is the issue.
dn-support: Support resists vertical force toward the tissues.
Vertical dislodgement away from the tissues is retention.
Rotation isn't one of the three definitions; support is vertical force toward the tissues.
dn-stability: Vertical force toward the tissues is support.
Dislodgement away from the tissues is retention.
Tooth wear affects vertical dimension, not the definition of stability.
dn-ssr-most: Stability is the most important: sliding sideways hurts and stops patients eating.
Retention bothers patients, but it doesn't hurt.
Support matters, but stability is the one he ranked first.
Esthetics isn't one of the three; stability is the most important of them.
dn-support-areas: The buccal shelf and retromolar pad below and the palate above are the primary support areas.
The ridges aren't good at taking support, and the premaxilla takes force poorly after tooth loss.
The floor of the mouth is movable tissue, not a support area.
The vestibule and lip are movable tissues beyond the peripheral border.
dn-premax: The premaxilla takes force poorly once the teeth are gone, so contacts stay posterior.
Material isn't the reason; anterior denture teeth are the same materials.
A facebow doesn't need anterior contact.
Vertical dimension is set with the rims, not by leaving the incisors free.
dn-co: Teeth fitted together with the joints seated is centric occlusion in a denture.
MIP is a neuromuscular position, not used for dentures.
The alert feeding position is head forward and down, a dentate concept.
Protrusive balance is contact while sliding forward, not the closed position.
dn-cr: Contracting elevators seat the condyles, with no teeth guiding the jaw elsewhere.
Ridges don't guide the mandible; the muscles seat the joints.
Denture teeth don't hold the condyles; muscle contraction seats them.
They can still protrude; most simply don't posture forward.
dn-bal-def: Balance: both sides, anterior and posterior, touching at once in centric and eccentric positions.
Contact in centric only is non-balanced occlusion.
Working-side canine contact is canine guidance for natural teeth.
Lingual cusps only, with no anterior contact, describes lingualized occlusion.
dn-nonbal-def: Non-balanced: flat teeth on a plane parallel to the ridges, no guidance, no compensating curve.
Teeth kept in contact in excursions on a compensating curve is balanced occlusion.
Protrusive balance with guiding anteriors is a balanced setup with anatomic teeth.
A compensating curve for left-right balance is balanced lingualized occlusion.
dn-cg0: Built at zero, the denture separates as the patient's real (never zero) guidance drops the condyles.
Matching the patient's path is what a balanced denture needs, not a non-balanced one.
Keeping contact in excursions is balance; zero guidance is used to lose it.
Non-balanced dentures have no anterior contact or guidance.
dn-nonbal-except: A compensating curve keeps teeth together: a tool of balance, not of non-balanced setups.
Zero condylar guidance lets the patient's real guidance separate the teeth.
Lingual positioning keeps the forces centered and off the buccal.
Narrower, flat teeth reduce lateral forces and contacts.
dn-m2: The ramus rises behind the first molar, so a flat plane can't continue there.
Support comes from the buccal shelf and pad, not from leaving teeth off.
The retromolar pad is a support area the base covers.
Articulator size isn't the reason; the rising ramus is.
dn-bolus: With food between the teeth there's no balance, and the denture can tip.
Balance needs tooth contact, and a bolus keeps the teeth apart.
The anterior teeth don't take over; incising food tips the denture.
Biting harder on a bolus increases tipping, not balance.
dn-chew: Both sides, chewing vertically, on the premolars: how denture patients avoid tipping.
Incising with the front teeth tips the back down and flips the lower denture up.
Chewing on one side tips the denture; food goes on both sides.
Big bites tip dentures; patients learn to avoid them.
dn-ling-def: An elongated maxillary lingual cusp against flat or wide-fossa lower teeth: a mortar and pestle.
It is the maxillary lingual cusp that is elongated, not a mandibular buccal cusp.
Full cusp-fossa contact of anatomic teeth is classic bilateral balance.
Flat teeth in both arches is non-balanced occlusion.
dn-ling-pop: It is much easier to arrange and works balanced or non-balanced.
Lingualized never has anterior contact; anatomic balanced teeth can.
Anatomic teeth in balance give the best esthetics.
Fewer contacts make wear show sooner, not slower.
dn-ling-ant: Balanced lingualized gives left-right balance only; it can't stop front-to-back tipping.
Anterior guidance tips a denture; lingualized never provides it.
There is no canine contact either.
Tooth material doesn't change the scheme.
